notes.meaning: God answers Moses' complaint by assuring him that Pharaoh will soon be forced to release the people. God's mighty power will be shown in judgments against Egypt, driving Pharaoh to let them go. Deliverance happens when God takes the matter into His own hands.

God speaks again to remind Moses of who He is: the Lord, the eternal and unchangeable God. This name means He is faithful to what He begins and always keeps His promises. Hearing this name gives Moses courage to keep going.

God made Himself known to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, showing them His power to make great promises. Now, as the Lord, He is revealing His character by actually fulfilling those ancient promises. The patriarchs had the promises, but Moses and Israel will see them carried out.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue this passage reflects a separate ancient document whose author believed God's personal name was completely unknown before Moses.

notes.meaning: God reminds Moses of the formal agreement, or covenant, He made with the patriarchs. He pledged to give them the land of Canaan, where they had lived only as wandering foreigners. This reminder proves that God has not forgotten His long-term plan for their family.

God hears the painful cries of the Israelites under cruel Egyptian slavery. When the Bible says God remembers His covenant, it means He is now stepping in to take action. He notices the suffering of His people and will not let their oppressors have the final word.

Moses is told to give Israel a message of full rescue from their heavy burdens. God promises to redeem them, acting like a family protector who steps in to free a helpless relative from slavery. He will show His great power openly through mighty judgments against Egypt.

God promises to take Israel as His special people and to be their God. The ultimate goal of saving them is not just freedom from work, but a close personal relationship with Him. Through this great rescue, the people will truly know Him by experience.

God promises to lead the people into the promised land that He swore to give their ancestors. Giving it as a permanent possession rests entirely on His own authority. He seals this guarantee by declaring once more, 'I am the Lord.'

Moses delivers God's wonderful promises to the people, but they are too crushed to listen. Their spirits are broken by harsh labor and deep disappointment after their work got worse. Severe pain and grief can make it very hard to take in good news.

God tells Moses to go back before Pharaoh and demand the complete release of Israel. This command is even stronger than the first request, calling for them to leave Egypt entirely. God patiently repeats His commands to leaders before He sends His judgments.

Moses shrinks back in discouragement, arguing that Pharaoh will never listen to him. If his own people refused to hear him, he expects an enemy king to be even more stubborn. He complains that he is clumsy in speech and unfit to speak for God.

God gives Moses and Aaron an official command for both the Israelites and Pharaoh. Instead of arguing with Moses' doubts, God issues a clear royal order that must be obeyed. His authority settles every excuse and sends the two brothers forward to finish the mission.

The account begins a family list to prove where Moses and Aaron came from among the tribes of Israel. It starts with Reuben, the firstborn son of Jacob, and lists his family heads. This shows that the deliverers of Israel were true members of the family of Abraham.

The family record continues with Simeon, Jacob's second son, and names his six sons. Listing these older brothers follows normal Hebrew custom before moving to the specific tribe of Moses and Aaron. It shows that each family line had an orderly place in the nation.

The record now comes to Levi, Jacob's third son and the forefather of Moses and Aaron. Levi's three sons are named, and his total age is given as 137 years. God blessed this family line with long life even before they became the priestly tribe.

Gershon was Levi's first son, and his two sons founded their own family branches. Though Gershon was the oldest, his line was not chosen for the high priesthood. God distributes His callings according to His own purpose rather than birth order.

Kohath was Levi's second son, and his descendants became the central branch of the Levites. His four sons are named, including Amram, and his lifespan of 133 years is recorded. It was from this family group that God chose the leaders who would bring Israel out of Egypt.

Merari was the third son of Levi, and his two sons headed their own family groups. This completes the overview of Levi's three main branches. The stage is now set to focus specifically on the family line of Aaron and Moses.

Amram married Jochebed, and they became the parents of Aaron and Moses. Marriages between close relatives happened in earlier times, though God's law later forbade them. Moses honestly recorded his family history without hiding anything uncomfortable.

differ.view: Some Methodist commentators hold that Jochebed was Amram's cousin or general kinswoman rather than his father's sister.
Baptist commentators read the text literally to mean Amram married his father's sister, his biological aunt.

notes.meaning: The sons of Kohath's second son, Izhar, are listed here. One of them is Korah, who would later lead a famous rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the desert. Moses faithfully included Korah in the family record even though Korah brought shame to the clan.

Kohath's son Uzziel had three sons, who were first cousins to Aaron and Moses. Two of them, Mishael and Elzaphan, would later be called to carry the bodies of Aaron's sons out of the camp when they died before the Lord. This note shows how closely connected the priestly leaders were to one another.

Aaron married Elisheba, a woman from the royal tribe of Judah whose brother was a leading prince. She gave birth to Aaron's four sons, who were designated for the priesthood. This union connected the priestly family of Levi with the royal family line of Judah.

Korah's three sons are listed as the heads of their own family lines. Although their father later rebelled against God, these sons did not share in his wickedness and survived. Their descendants went on to serve faithfully in the worship of the temple.

Aaron's son Eleazar married and had a son named Phinehas, who became famous for his zeal for God. This verse traces the high priestly line from Aaron directly to his grandson. It concludes the family list of the Levite leaders.

The narrative stresses that this very Aaron and Moses were the ones God called to lead Israel out of Egypt. They were not mysterious figures from nowhere, but known members of their own people. God planned to march the Israelites out in orderly groups like organized armies.

The writer repeats that Moses and Aaron were the exact men who spoke directly to Pharaoh. By naming them again, the record highlights their God-given role as the deliverers of the nation. It confirms their authority as God's official spokesmen.

The story returns to where it stopped before the family list, repeating God's direct command to Moses. God reminds Moses of His divine name and charges him to speak every single word God gives him to the king of Egypt. A true messenger from God must deliver the whole message faithfully without holding anything back.

Moses once again objects that he speaks poorly and doubts Pharaoh will ever listen to him. This repetition shows how deeply discouraged Moses felt about his own abilities. It also highlights that Israel's deliverance would be accomplished by God's power alone, not human eloquence.
